records.source: Οὐ θέλω γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοί, ὅτι οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν πάντες ὑπὸ τὴν νεφέλην ἦσαν καὶ πάντες διὰ τῆς θαλάσσης διῆλθον, καὶ πάντες εἰς τὸν Μωϋσῆν ἐβαπτίσαντο ἐν τῇ νεφέλῃ καὶ ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ, καὶ πάντες τὸ αὐτὸ πνευματικὸν βρῶμα ἔφαγον καὶ πάντες τὸ αὐτὸ πνευματικὸν ἔπιον πόμα, ἔπινον γὰρ ἐκ πνευματικῆς ἀκολουθούσης πέτρας, ἡ πέτρα δὲ ἦν ὁ Χριστός·
records.gloss: Not I want for you to be ignorant, brothers, that the fathers of us all under the cloud were and all through the sea passed, \v 2 and all into the Moses were baptized in the cloud and in the sea, \v 3 and all the same spiritual food ate \v 4 and all the same spiritual drank drink; they were drinking for from a spiritual following rock, the rock but was the Christ;
pieces: For I want you to grasp this, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}: every one of our ancestors was under the cloud, and every one of them went through the sea.
All of them were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.
All of them ate the same spiritual food,
and all of them drank the same spiritual drink. They drank from a spiritual rock that went along with them, and that rock was {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.1: For I do not want you to be unaware, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea,
L.2: and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
L.3: and all ate the same spiritual food,
L.4: and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they kept drinking from a spiritual rock that followed [them], and the rock was the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.1: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I want you to know what happened to our ancestors, the people of Israel, when Moses led them out of Egypt. The cloud of God's presence was over all of them, and all of them walked through the sea.
R.2: In the cloud and in the sea, all of them were baptized into Moses, and so they were joined to him as their leader.
R.3: All of them ate the same spiritual food that God gave them,
R.4: and all of them drank the same spiritual drink. They drank from a spiritual rock that went along with them, and that rock was {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: for: the story of Israel backs up the warning at the end of chapter 9
alternatives: a loose link marking a new subject
decisions.reason: In 9:24-27 Paul warns that a runner can lose the prize, and that he disciplines himself so that he will not be disqualified. γὰρ introduces the proof: Israel had every privilege, and still most of them fell (verse 5).

decisions.choice: under the cloud ... through the sea: the cloud that led Israel out of Egypt and the crossing of the Red Sea
decisions.reason: Exodus 13:21-22 and 14:19-22 tell of the pillar of cloud that went with the people and stood between them and the Egyptians, and of the sea that God divided so that they crossed on dry ground. Psalm 105:39 speaks of the cloud spread over them.

decisions.choice: baptized into Moses: by passing under the cloud and through the water, Israel was joined to Moses as its leader, as believers are joined to Christ in baptism
alternatives: only a figure of speech with no link to Christian baptism
decisions.reason: No Israelite was immersed: they crossed on dry ground. Paul describes the Exodus in the language of Christian baptism ("baptized into Christ", Romans 6:3; Galatians 3:27; compare 1:13 here) to show that Israel had its own version of the church's privileges. The point is the warning: those privileges did not protect them.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: ἐβαπτίσαντο, the middle form ("they had themselves baptized" or simply "were baptized")
alternatives: the passive form ("were baptized"), found in other manuscripts
decisions.reason: Both forms are well attested in the manuscripts and the sense is the same: "were baptized". The SBLGNT text governs. The evidence here is described from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: spiritual: given by God through his Spirit, and pointing beyond itself to what believers receive
alternatives: symbolic only, not real food and drink
decisions.reason: The food was the manna (Exodus 16; Psalm 78:24-25) and the drink was the water from the rock (Exodus 17:1-7; Numbers 20:2-13): real food and water, but given by God in a way that went beyond nature. πνευματικὸν is the word Paul uses for what comes from the Spirit (2:13-15). The food and drink point ahead to the bread and cup of the Lord's Supper (verses 16-17).

decisions.choice: a rock that followed them: the rock that gave water at the start and the end of the wilderness journey, which Paul pictures as going with Israel
alternatives: a rock that only stood in one place
decisions.reason: Water came from a rock near the start of the journey (Exodus 17:6) and again near its end (Numbers 20:7-11). Later Jewish writings tell of a well that went with Israel through the wilderness. Paul's "followed" may draw on that story, but his point is not the legend: the source of their drink was always with them.

decisions.choice: the rock was Christ: Christ himself was present with Israel in the wilderness, giving them drink
alternatives: the rock represented or pictured Christ
decisions.reason: The verb is "was", in the past: Paul does not say the rock "stands for" Christ. In the Song of Moses God is called "the Rock" of Israel (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 18, 30-31). Paul names Christ as that Rock, present and active before he came as a man (compare 8:6, where all things exist through him). Verse 9 draws the consequence: Israel could put Christ to the test.

decisions.choice: our fathers: Israel's ancestors are the ancestors of believers, Gentiles included
alternatives: the ancestors of Jewish believers only
decisions.reason: Most of the Corinthian church had been pagans (12:2), yet Paul calls the wilderness generation "our fathers". Those who belong to Christ share Israel's story (compare Galatians 3:7, 29).

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: ἀδελφοί addresses the whole church, women and men (terms doc).

decisions.choice: every one of ... All of them (B); all of them (R)
decisions.reason: Paul says "all" five times: every Israelite had the privileges, yet most fell (verse 5). Balanced and Readable make the repetition heard.

decisions.choice: ancestors (B, R); fathers (L)
decisions.reason: The word means the earlier generations of the people, men and women alike. "Ancestors" says that plainly, as in John 6:31.

decisions.choice: the people of Israel, when Moses led them out of Egypt; The cloud of God's presence; joined to him as their leader; that God gave them
decisions.reason: Readable names the people and the event, and explains "baptized into Moses" (m3) and "spiritual" (m5).

records.heading: Warnings from Israel's history

records.source: ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐν τοῖς πλείοσιν αὐτῶν ηὐδόκησεν ὁ θεός, κατεστρώθησαν γὰρ ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ.
records.gloss: But not with the most of them was well pleased the God, they were strewn for in the wilderness.
pieces: Yet God took no pleasure in most of them, for the wilderness was strewn with their bodies.

L.5: But with most of them God was not well pleased, for they were strewn [dead] in the wilderness.

R.5: But most of them did not please God. They died in the desert, and their bodies were left lying there.

decisions.choice: strewn in the wilderness: the death of the whole adult generation in the wilderness, as God had said
decisions.reason: In Numbers 14:16 and 14:29-35 God says that the bodies of those who refused to enter the land will fall in the wilderness. κατεστρώθησαν is the verb of Numbers 14:16 in the Greek Old Testament. Of the adults who left Egypt only Joshua and Caleb entered the land.

decisions.choice: not with most of them: an understatement; almost all of them
decisions.reason: "Not ... most" is a restrained way of saying that nearly the whole generation came under God's judgment (Numbers 14:29-30).

decisions.choice: for: their death in the wilderness shows that God was not pleased with them
decisions.reason: γὰρ gives the evidence for the first clause, not its cause.

decisions.choice: the wilderness was strewn with their bodies
alternatives: they were struck down in the wilderness
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of the verb, bodies scattered across the ground, and turns it round so that the sentence reads naturally.

decisions.choice: desert
decisions.reason: Readable uses the common word; the place was dry, empty land.

records.source: Ταῦτα δὲ τύποι ἡμῶν ἐγενήθησαν, εἰς τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἐπιθυμητὰς κακῶν, καθὼς κἀκεῖνοι ἐπεθύμησαν.
records.gloss: These things now examples of us became, for the not to be us desirers of evil things, as those also desired.
pieces: These events became examples for us, warning us not to crave what is evil, as they craved it.

L.6: Now these things became examples for us, so that we would not be people who desire evil things, as they also desired.

R.6: What happened to them is a warning for us. We must not long for evil things the way they did.

decisions.choice: examples: events that serve as patterns and warnings for the church
alternatives: types in a technical sense, events that predict later ones
decisions.reason: τύποι is a mark left by a blow, then a pattern or model. Here what happened to Israel is a pattern that God intended to speak to the church, and in this passage it speaks as a warning. Verse 11 says the same with the adverb τυπικῶς.

decisions.choice: for us: for our benefit, as a lesson aimed at us
alternatives: examples of us, that is, pictures of what we are
decisions.reason: The genitive ἡμῶν is best taken as "for us", as verse 11 says plainly: "written down to warn us".

decisions.choice: they craved: the people's craving for meat in the wilderness
decisions.reason: In Numbers 11:4-34 the people crave meat, and the place where they were buried is named "Graves of Craving". This craving heads a list of five sins (verses 6-10); the first and last echo the Corinthians' own appetite for temple meals.

decisions.choice: examples ... warning (B); a warning (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps "examples" and makes their purpose explicit (m1); Readable says simply what they are for.

decisions.choice: crave ... craved (B); long for (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced repeats the verb as the Greek repeats the root, and "crave" recalls the craving for meat in Numbers 11 (m3).

records.source: μηδὲ εἰδωλολάτραι γίνεσθε, καθώς τινες αὐτῶν· ὥσπερ γέγραπται· Ἐκάθισεν ὁ λαὸς φαγεῖν καὶ πεῖν, καὶ ἀνέστησαν παίζειν.
records.gloss: Neither idolaters become, as some of them; as it has been written: Sat the people to eat and to drink, and rose up to play.
pieces: Do not become idolaters, as some of them did. Scripture says, "The people sat down to eat and drink, and then rose to make merry."

L.7: Do not become idolaters either, as some of them [were]; as it is written, "The people sat to eat and to drink, and they rose up to play."

R.7: Do not worship idols, as some of them did. The Scriptures say, "The people sat down to eat and drink. Then they got up and celebrated with wild dancing."

decisions.choice: a quotation of Exodus 32:6, the feast before the golden calf
decisions.reason: Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament of Exodus 32:6 word for word. The people made a golden calf, offered sacrifices to it, and then held a feast in its honor (Exodus 32:1-6, 17-19).

decisions.choice: eat and drink in honor of an idol: the same thing as the Corinthians' meals in idol temples
decisions.reason: Paul chooses the one verse that joins idolatry and a sacrificial meal. Those in Corinth who ate in an idol's temple (8:10) were doing what Israel did at Sinai.

decisions.choice: play: festive dancing and revelry in the idol's honor
decisions.reason: παίζειν is used in the Greek Old Testament for dancing and festivity, and in Exodus 32:19 Moses sees the calf and the dancing. Some read a sexual sense into it, which would lead into verse 8, but the text does not require it.

decisions.choice: do not become: a command to the Corinthians, after the "we" of verse 6
decisions.reason: Paul moves between "you" (verses 7, 10) and "let us" (verses 8-9), but the warnings are one series.

decisions.choice: make merry (B); celebrated with wild dancing (R)
decisions.reason: "Play" now suggests children's games. Balanced uses an older but clear word for festive celebration; Readable names the dancing (m3).

decisions.choice: Scripture says (B); The Scriptures say (R)
decisions.reason: The formula introduces a quotation from Scripture, so Balanced and Readable say so plainly.

decisions.choice: worship idols
decisions.reason: As in the vice lists of 5:10-11 and 6:9 (terms doc).

records.source: μηδὲ πορνεύωμεν, καθώς τινες αὐτῶν ἐπόρνευσαν, καὶ ἔπεσαν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ εἴκοσι τρεῖς χιλιάδες.
records.gloss: Neither let us commit sexual immorality, as some of them committed sexual immorality, and fell in one day twenty three thousand.
pieces: Nor should we give ourselves to sexual immorality, which some of them practiced, and 23,000 fell dead in a single day.

L.8: Neither let us commit sexual immorality, as some of them committed sexual immorality, and 23,000 fell in one day.

R.8: We must not commit sexual sins, as some of them did. Because of that, 23,000 of them died in one day.

decisions.choice: Israel at Peor: sexual sin with Moabite women that led to the worship of their god
decisions.reason: In Numbers 25:1-9 Israelite men had sex with Moabite women, who invited them to the sacrifices of their gods; the people ate and bowed down to Baal of Peor, and a plague followed. Idolatry, sacrificial meals and sexual sin came together, as they could at Corinthian temple feasts (compare 6:12-20).

decisions.choice: twenty-three thousand: Numbers 25:9 gives twenty-four thousand
decisions.reason: Paul's number is one thousand lower than Numbers 25:9. He may be giving a round figure from memory, or counting only those who died "in one day". Exodus 32:28 tells of three thousand who died after the golden calf, and some think Paul's figure combines the two stories. The text does not explain the difference.

decisions.choice: commit sexual immorality: any sexual relationship outside marriage
decisions.reason: The verb belongs with πορνεύω's noun, sexual immorality (5:1; 6:13, 18).

decisions.choice: let us: Paul includes himself in the warning
decisions.reason: The first person plural shows that no one is above the warning, Paul included (9:27).
Numbers above ninety-nine are written in figures (style guide).

decisions.choice: Because of that
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that the deaths were God's judgment on their sin (Numbers 25:9).

decisions.choice: give ourselves to sexual immorality, which some of them practiced
alternatives: commit sexual immorality, as some of them did
decisions.reason: Balanced avoids repeating the verb and keeps "sexual immorality" (terms doc); Readable says "sexual sins".

records.source: μηδὲ ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν Χριστόν, καθώς τινες αὐτῶν ἐπείρασαν, καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ὄφεων ἀπώλλυντο.
records.gloss: Neither let us put to the test the Christ, as some of them tested, and by the serpents they were being destroyed.
pieces: Nor should we try the patience of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, as some of them tried it; they were killed off by the snakes, one after another.

L.9: Neither let us put the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} to the test, as some of them tested [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}], and they were destroyed by the serpents.

R.9: We must not try to see how far we can push {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, as some of them did. Snakes bit them, and they died.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "Christ"
alternatives: "the Lord", found in other early manuscripts
decisions.reason: The manuscripts differ here. "Christ" is found in the earliest papyrus and in many later manuscripts; several important early manuscripts read "the Lord", and a few "God". "Christ" is the harder reading, since a copyist would more readily change a statement that Israel tested Christ than create one, and it fits verse 4. The SBLGNT text governs. The evidence here is described from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: Israel put Christ to the test: Christ was present with Israel in the wilderness
decisions.reason: Verse 4 has already said that the rock was Christ. Testing God in the wilderness (Psalm 78:18; 95:9) was therefore testing Christ, and the Corinthians are in danger of doing the same.

decisions.choice: the serpents: Numbers 21:4-9
decisions.reason: The people spoke against God and Moses, complaining about the manna, and God sent poisonous snakes among them, so that many died.

decisions.choice: put to the test: provoke God by demanding that he prove himself, to see how far one can go
decisions.reason: ἐκπειράζωμεν is a strengthened form of πειράζω. To test God is to challenge his patience and faithfulness instead of trusting him (Deuteronomy 6:16). For the Corinthians it would mean going on eating at idol feasts as if the Lord would not care (verse 22).

decisions.choice: were destroyed: the imperfect tense pictures the deaths going on, one after another
decisions.reason: ἀπώλλυντο is imperfect, unlike the single act of the other verbs.

decisions.choice: try the patience of (B); try to see how far we can push (R)
decisions.reason: In current speech "test" can sound like an exam; Balanced and Readable say what testing God means here (m4).

decisions.choice: [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}]
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the object, a pronoun for Christ.

records.source: μηδὲ γογγύζετε, καθάπερ τινὲς αὐτῶν ἐγόγγυσαν, καὶ ἀπώλοντο ὑπὸ τοῦ ὀλοθρευτοῦ.
records.gloss: Neither grumble, as some of them grumbled, and perished by the Destroyer.
pieces: Do not grumble against God, the way some of them grumbled, only to perish at the hand of the Destroyer.

L.10: Nor grumble, as some of them grumbled, and they perished by the Destroyer.

R.10: Do not complain against God, as some of them did. The angel God sent to bring death destroyed them.

decisions.choice: the grumbling of Israel in the wilderness, and the death that followed
decisions.reason: Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron, and so against God, again and again (Exodus 16:2-12; Numbers 14:2, 27, 36). After the revolt of Korah the whole people grumbled, and a plague killed thousands (Numbers 16:41-49). Paul may have either story in mind.

decisions.choice: the Destroyer: the angel God sends to carry out his judgment
alternatives: a demon acting on its own
decisions.reason: ὀλοθρευτοῦ recalls "the destroyer" who struck Egypt on the night of the Passover (Exodus 12:23) and the destroying angel of 2 Samuel 24:16 and 1 Chronicles 21:15. The Numbers stories speak of a plague; Paul names the one who brought it.

decisions.choice: grumble: complain with resentment, accusing God of failing his people
decisions.reason: γογγύζετε is the word for Israel's grumbling in the Greek Old Testament. Paul uses a command, "do not grumble", as he did in verse 7.

decisions.choice: against God
decisions.reason: In the stories Paul recalls, grumbling against Moses was grumbling against God (Exodus 16:8; Numbers 14:27).

decisions.choice: The angel God sent to bring death
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the Destroyer was (m2).

records.source: ταῦτα δὲ τυπικῶς συνέβαινεν ἐκείνοις, ἐγράφη δὲ πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν, εἰς οὓς τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων κατήντηκεν.
records.gloss: These things now as examples were happening to those, were written but for admonition of us, to whom the ends of the ages have arrived.
pieces: What happened to them was meant as an example, and it was written down to warn us, who live at the time when the ages reach their end.

L.11: Now these things kept happening to them by way of example, and they were written for our warning, to whom the ends of the ages have arrived.

R.11: What happened to them was an example. It was written down as a warning for us, because we are living at the time when everything God planned for all the ages is coming to its goal.

decisions.choice: as examples: in a way that makes them patterns and warnings
decisions.reason: τυπικῶς picks up τύποι from verse 6 (m1 there): God shaped these events to speak to later generations.

decisions.choice: warning: instruction that corrects and puts a person on guard
decisions.reason: νουθεσίαν is instruction aimed at changing behavior, often a warning (compare Ephesians 6:4).

decisions.choice: the ends of the ages have come: believers live at the time when the ages reach their goal in Christ
alternatives: the end of the world is about to happen
the end of the old age overlapping the start of the new
decisions.reason: Since Christ came, history has reached its last stage, the time God's promises looked toward. The plural "ends" may picture all the earlier ages reaching their goal together. Because the church lives at this decisive time, the Scriptures about Israel were written with it in view (compare Romans 15:4).

decisions.choice: kept happening: the imperfect tense pictures the events one after another
decisions.reason: συνέβαινεν is imperfect; ἐγράφη is a single act, "were written".

decisions.choice: who live at the time when the ages reach their end
alternatives: on whom the ends of the ages have come
decisions.reason: The literal phrase is hard to follow; Balanced says what it means while keeping "the ages".

decisions.choice: because we are living at the time when everything God planned for all the ages is coming to its goal
decisions.reason: Readable explains the phrase (m3) and makes the link to "warning for us" explicit.

records.source: ὥστε ὁ δοκῶν ἑστάναι βλεπέτω μὴ πέσῃ, πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος· πιστὸς δὲ ὁ θεός, ὃς οὐκ ἐάσει ὑμᾶς πειρασθῆναι ὑπὲρ ὃ δύνασθε, ἀλλὰ ποιήσει σὺν τῷ πειρασμῷ καὶ τὴν ἔκβασιν τοῦ δύνασθαι ὑπενεγκεῖν.
records.gloss: So that the [one] thinking to stand let him watch lest he fall. \v 13 Testing you not has taken except human; faithful but [is] the God, who not will allow you to be tested beyond what you are able, but will make with the testing also the way out of the to be able to endure.
pieces: So anyone who feels sure of standing should watch out, or {{gender:they|he}} may fall.

The testing that has gripped you is only what all people face. But God is faithful, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will not allow the testing to go past your strength. Along with the testing {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will also make the way out, so that you are able to hold up under it.

L.12: So let the one who thinks {{gender:they stand|he stands}} watch out lest {{gender:they|he}} fall.
L.13: No testing has taken hold of you except [what is] human; but God [is] faithful, who will not let you be tested beyond what you are able, but with the testing will also make the way out, so that you are able to bear [it].

R.12: So if you think you are standing strong, be careful. You too could fall.
R.13: The tests you face are the same kind that all people face. But you can trust God. He will not let you be tested more than you can stand. When a test comes, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will also open a way through it for you, and you will be able to stand up under it.

decisions.choice: the one who thinks he stands: anyone confident of his own spiritual safety
decisions.reason: δοκῶν often means to think something of oneself, perhaps wrongly (3:18; 8:2). Those with "knowledge" who ate in idol temples (8:10) may be in view, but the warning is general: Israel too was sure of its privileges.

decisions.choice: testing: any trial that puts faith under pressure, including the pull to give in and sin
alternatives: temptation, the inner pull toward sin alone
decisions.reason: πειρασμὸς and πειρασθῆναι cover both a hard trial and an enticement to do wrong. Here the pressure is above all the social pull of idol feasts. The same root was used in verse 9: Israel "tested" Christ; now Paul speaks of the testing that comes on believers, which God limits.

decisions.choice: human: common to human beings, the kind of trial people normally face
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπινος means "belonging to humans". The Corinthians' trials are not unique or beyond the ordinary.

decisions.choice: God is faithful: God keeps faith with his people and sets limits to what they face
decisions.reason: As in 1:9, God's faithfulness is the ground of confidence. Testing does not come apart from his care: he does not let it go beyond what his people can bear.

decisions.choice: the way out ... to endure: a way through the testing, so that believers can bear it, not escape all trial
decisions.reason: ἔκβασιν is a way out or outcome. The purpose clause, δύνασθαι ὑπενεγκεῖν, shows that the way out is the power to endure. For the Corinthians the way out of idolatry is to flee it (verse 14).

decisions.choice: the warning and the promise belong together
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT joins verses 12 and 13 with a comma. Verse 13 is not a new subject: the confident are warned, and the anxious are reassured that the testing can be withstood.

decisions.choice: testing, tested (L, B); tests, tested (R)
decisions.reason: "Testing" keeps the link with verse 9 and the wider sense of the word (m2); a footnote gives "temptation".

decisions.choice: {{gender:they stand|he stands}}; {{gender:they|he}}
decisions.reason: The participle means anyone, man or woman. Readable speaks to "you" and needs no setting.

decisions.choice: gripped
decisions.reason: εἴληφεν means "has taken hold of"; "gripped" keeps the picture of being seized.

decisions.choice: you can trust God
decisions.reason: Readable says what "faithful" means for the reader.

records.source: Διόπερ, ἀγαπητοί μου, φεύγετε ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδωλολατρίας.
records.gloss: Therefore, beloved of me, flee from the idolatry.
pieces: So then, my dear friends, run from idolatry.

L.14: For this reason, my beloved, flee from idolatry.

R.14: So, my dear friends, stay far away from worshiping idols.

decisions.choice: for this reason: because God gives a way out of testing (verse 13), and because of Israel's example (verses 1-12)
decisions.reason: Διόπερ draws the conclusion of the whole section. The way out that God gives is to be taken: run from idolatry.

decisions.choice: idolatry: here above all taking part in sacrificial meals in honor of idols
decisions.reason: Verses 16-22 show what Paul means: eating at the table of a pagan god in its temple. The present imperative φεύγετε calls for a settled habit of avoiding it.

decisions.choice: my beloved: people Paul loves, and whom God loves
decisions.reason: The address softens the sharp command and recalls 4:14, where Paul calls them his beloved children.

decisions.choice: my dear friends
decisions.reason: As in 2 Corinthians 7:1 and Philippians 4:1; "beloved" is rare in speech today.

decisions.choice: run from (B); stay far away from (R)
decisions.reason: Both keep the urgency of the verb in everyday words.

records.heading: The Lord's table and the table of demons

records.source: ὡς φρονίμοις λέγω· κρίνατε ὑμεῖς ὅ φημι.
records.gloss: As to sensible [people] I speak; judge you what I say.
pieces: I am talking to you as people with good sense. Weigh for yourselves what I am saying.

L.15: As to sensible [people] I speak; you yourselves judge what I am saying.

R.15: You are wise enough to understand this. So think about what I am saying, and decide for yourselves.

decisions.choice: sensible: able to think a matter through and see where it leads
decisions.reason: φρονίμοις is a person of practical good sense. In 4:10 Paul used the word with irony, but here he appeals to their judgment, sure that they will see the force of the argument that follows.

decisions.choice: you yourselves: the pronoun is emphatic
decisions.reason: ὑμεῖς is stated with the verb: Paul invites them to judge for themselves.

decisions.choice: Weigh
decisions.reason: "Judge" can sound like passing sentence; the sense is to assess.

records.source: τὸ ποτήριον τῆς εὐλογίας ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν, οὐχὶ κοινωνία ἐστὶν τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ;
records.gloss: The cup of the blessing that we bless, not a sharing is it of the blood of the Christ?
pieces: When we bless the cup of blessing, are we not given a share in the blood of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}?

L.16: The cup of the blessing which we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}?

R.16: When we thank God over the cup and drink from it, we share in the blood of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death for us.

decisions.choice: the cup of blessing: the cup of wine over which thanks to God was said at a Jewish meal, and so the cup of the Lord's Supper
decisions.reason: At a Jewish meal, and at the Passover in particular, a cup of wine was blessed with thanks to God after the meal. Jesus took the cup "after supper" (11:25). "We bless" means that the church gives thanks to God over the cup.

decisions.choice: sharing: having a real part, together with others, in what Christ's death has won, and being joined to him
alternatives: only a symbol of the blood
decisions.reason: κοινωνία is having something in common with others. In 1:9 believers are called into the κοινωνία of the Son, and in Philippians 3:10 Paul speaks of sharing in Christ's sufferings. Here those who drink the cup share together in Christ himself and the benefits of his death. Verses 18 and 20 apply the same idea to Israel's altar and to demons.

decisions.choice: the blood of Christ: his death, given for others
decisions.reason: Blood stands for life given up in death, as in 11:25, "the new covenant in my blood".

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: οὐχὶ introduces a question to which the Corinthians must agree; Paul builds his argument on what they already accept.

decisions.choice: the cup comes before the bread
alternatives: the order of the meal in Corinth
decisions.reason: In 11:23-26, as in the Gospels, the bread comes first. Here Paul names the cup first, probably so that he can go on from the bread to the one body (verse 17).

decisions.choice: a sharing in (L); given a share in (B); share in (R)
decisions.reason: "Communion" is now mainly a name for the Lord's Supper, and "participation" is abstract. "Share" is plain and can be used in verses 18 and 20 too.

decisions.choice: thank God over the cup and drink from it; in his death for us
decisions.reason: Readable explains the blessing (m1) and what "blood" means (m3), and turns the question into the statement it expects (m4).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}
decisions.reason: A pronoun for Christ.

records.source: τὸν ἄρτον ὃν κλῶμεν, οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐστιν;
records.gloss: The bread that we break, not a sharing of the body of the Christ is it?
pieces: When we break the bread, are we not given a share in the body of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}?

L.16: The bread which we break, is it not a sharing in the body of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}?

R.16: And when we break the bread and eat it, we share in the body of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: the bread that we break: the loaf broken and shared at the Lord's Supper
decisions.reason: At a Jewish meal the host gave thanks and broke the bread to share it, as Jesus did at the Last Supper (11:23-24).

decisions.choice: the body of Christ: his body given in death, which also leads to the church as his body
alternatives: the bread changed into his body
decisions.reason: In 11:24 "my body, which is for you" is Christ's own body given up in death. The next verse moves straight on to the church as "one body", so Paul may already have both in mind. The text does not explain how the bread and the body are related, only that eating it gives a share in him.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: As in the first half of the verse.

decisions.choice: a sharing in (L); given a share in (B); share in (R)
decisions.reason: As in the first half of the verse (16.s1, r-en-1).

records.source: ὅτι εἷς ἄρτος, ἓν σῶμα οἱ πολλοί ἐσμεν, οἱ γὰρ πάντες ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἄρτου μετέχομεν.
records.gloss: Because one bread, one body the many we are, the for all from the one bread we partake.
pieces: There is one loaf, and so we, though many, are one body, because we all share in that one loaf.

L.17: Because [there is] one loaf, we, the many, are one body; for all of us partake from the one loaf.

R.17: There is only one loaf of bread. So all of us, even though there are many of us, are one body, because we all eat from that one loaf.

decisions.choice: because there is one loaf, we the many are one body: the one loaf is the reason they are one body
alternatives: "for we, many as we are, are one bread and one body", with both nouns describing the church
the first clause completes verse 16: "since the bread is one"
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb in the first clause. The last clause, "for all of us partake from the one loaf", explains how one loaf makes one body, which supports reading the first clause as the reason.

decisions.choice: one body: the church, united as the body of Christ by sharing in him
decisions.reason: Chapter 12 develops the picture (12:12-27). Sharing one loaf at the Lord's Table binds believers to one another as well as to Christ; this is why they cannot also eat at the table of demons (verse 21).

decisions.choice: partake from: eat a share of the one loaf
decisions.reason: μετέχομεν means to have a share in something; with "from" it means eating a portion of the loaf.

decisions.choice: loaf
decisions.reason: ἄρτος is the same word as "bread" in verse 16, but here Paul means one loaf; "one bread" is not natural.

records.source: βλέπετε τὸν Ἰσραὴλ κατὰ σάρκα· οὐχ οἱ ἐσθίοντες τὰς θυσίας κοινωνοὶ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου εἰσίν;
records.gloss: Look at the Israel according to flesh; not those eating the sacrifices sharers of the altar are?
pieces: Look at Israel, the nation by human descent. Do not the people who eat from the sacrifices share in the altar?

L.18: Look at Israel according to flesh: those who eat the sacrifices, are they not sharers in the altar?

R.18: Think about the people of Israel. When they eat meat from the animals offered on the altar, they are taking part in the worship offered there.

decisions.choice: Israel according to the flesh: the people of Israel by physical descent, in their ordinary worship
alternatives: unfaithful Israel, such as those who worshiped the golden calf
decisions.reason: κατὰ σάρκα distinguishes the nation by birth from the wider people of God in Christ (compare Romans 9:3-8). Paul is not condemning Israel's sacrifices here; he uses them to show what eating a sacrifice means.

decisions.choice: those who eat the sacrifices: worshipers and priests who ate part of the offered animal
decisions.reason: In some of Israel's offerings part of the animal was burned on the altar and the rest eaten by the priests and the worshipers (Leviticus 7:11-18; Deuteronomy 12:17-18; compare 9:13).

decisions.choice: sharers in the altar: partners in the worship offered at the altar, and so with the God to whom it is offered
alternatives: sharing only the food from the altar
decisions.reason: κοινωνοὶ is a partner, someone who shares with others. The altar stands for the God worshiped there. The same word is used of demons in verse 20.

decisions.choice: the nation by human descent
decisions.reason: As the terms doc does for σάρξ elsewhere, Balanced gives the sense.

decisions.choice: When they eat meat from the animals offered on the altar, they are taking part in the worship offered there
decisions.reason: Readable explains the sacrifices (m2) and what sharing in the altar means (m3), and turns the question into the statement it expects.

records.source: τί οὖν φημι;
records.gloss: What then do I say?
pieces: What am I saying, then?

R.19: What do I mean by this?

decisions.choice: Paul heads off a misunderstanding of verses 16-18
decisions.reason: If eating a sacrifice makes one a partner in the altar, someone might think Paul is now saying that idols are real gods. The next question rejects that.

records.source: ὅτι εἰδωλόθυτόν τί ἐστιν, ἢ ὅτι εἴδωλόν τί ἐστιν;
records.gloss: That [food] offered to an idol anything is, or that an idol anything is?
pieces: That food offered to idols amounts to anything? Or that an idol is anything at all?

L.19: That [food] offered to idols is something, or that an idol is something?

R.19: Am I saying that food offered to idols is special in some way? Or that an idol is a real god?

decisions.choice: anything: anything real or of importance
decisions.reason: Paul does not take back what he agreed in 8:4: an idol is nothing. The food is just food, and the idol is not a god.

decisions.choice: questions that expect the answer no
decisions.reason: Verse 20 begins with ἀλλ: "no, rather".

decisions.choice: [food] offered to idols (L); food offered to idols (B, R)
decisions.reason: As throughout chapters 8-10 (terms doc).

records.source: ἀλλ’ ὅτι ἃ θύουσιν, δαιμονίοις καὶ οὐ θεῷ θύουσιν, οὐ θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς κοινωνοὺς τῶν δαιμονίων γίνεσθαι.
records.gloss: But that what they sacrifice, to demons and not to God they sacrifice; not I want but you sharers of the demons to become.
pieces: No. I mean that what people sacrifice to idols, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. And I do not want you to become partners with demons.

L.20: But that what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God; and I do not want you to become sharers with the demons.

R.20: No. But when people offer sacrifices to idols, they are really offering them to demons, not to God. And I do not want you to join in with demons.

decisions.choice: they sacrifice to demons and not to God: the words of Deuteronomy 32:17
decisions.reason: In the Song of Moses Israel "sacrificed to demons and not to God" (Deuteronomy 32:17 in the Greek Old Testament). The phrase can also be read "to what is not God". Paul uses the words of Scripture for pagan worship in Corinth. Verse 22 echoes the same song.

decisions.choice: demons: evil spiritual beings opposed to God
alternatives: the gods of the pagans, thought of as real
decisions.reason: The idol is nothing (verse 19), but the worship given to it is not neutral: spiritual powers opposed to God stand behind it. δαιμονίοις is the usual word for evil spirits in the Gospels.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "what they sacrifice", with no stated subject
alternatives: "what the Gentiles sacrifice", with the words "the Gentiles" added, found in many manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add a subject, "the Gentiles"; others, including early ones, lack it. The meaning is the same either way: the sacrifices of pagan worship. The SBLGNT text governs. The evidence here is described from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: partners: people who share in something with others
decisions.reason: κοινωνοὺς is the word of verse 18 ("sharers in the altar"). Eating at a sacrificial meal joins a person to the one worshiped there.

decisions.choice: people ... to idols
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the subject unstated (m3); Balanced and Readable say who is meant.

decisions.choice: partners (B); join in with (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "sharers", as in verse 18; Balanced uses a word that suits people sharing a meal and a loyalty.

records.source: οὐ δύνασθε ποτήριον κυρίου πίνειν καὶ ποτήριον δαιμονίων· οὐ δύνασθε τραπέζης κυρίου μετέχειν καὶ τραπέζης δαιμονίων.
records.gloss: Not you are able cup of Lord to drink and cup of demons; not you are able of table of Lord to partake and of table of demons.
pieces: It is impossible for you to drink from the Lord's cup and from a cup of demons as well, or to eat at the Lord's table and at a demons' table.

L.21: You are not able to drink a cup of [the] Lord and a cup of demons; you are not able to share in a table of [the] Lord and a table of demons.

R.21: You cannot drink from the Lord's cup and also from the cup used to honor demons. You cannot eat at the Lord's table and also at a table where demons are honored.

decisions.choice: the table of demons: meals in honor of a pagan god in its temple
decisions.reason: Papyrus invitations survive in which a person is invited "to dine at the table of the lord Sarapis". Pagan meals were held in the god's name, with the god thought of as host. The table of the Lord is the Lord's Supper, where Christ is the host.

decisions.choice: the table of the Lord: the altar of the Lord in Malachi
decisions.reason: Malachi 1:7, 12 calls the altar "the table of the LORD"; there the Hebrew has the divine name. Here "Lord" is the Lord Jesus, whose cup and bread are shared in verse 16.

decisions.choice: cannot: the two are incompatible, not physically impossible
decisions.reason: Some Corinthians did both. Paul means that a person cannot belong to both at once: loyalty to the Lord excludes taking part in the worship of other powers.

decisions.choice: It is impossible for you
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the force of "you are not able" (m3) and joins the two halves into one sentence.

decisions.choice: the cup used to honor demons; a table where demons are honored
decisions.reason: Readable explains the phrase "of demons" (m1).

records.source: ἢ παραζηλοῦμεν τὸν κύριον;
records.gloss: Or do we provoke to jealousy the Lord?
pieces: Or do we mean to stir up the Lord's jealousy?

L.22: Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy?

R.22: Do we really want to make the Lord jealous?

decisions.choice: provoke to jealousy: Deuteronomy 32:21, where Israel provoked God to jealousy with idols
decisions.reason: In the Song of Moses God says that Israel made him jealous with what is no god (Deuteronomy 32:16, 21). Paul has just used the same song in verse 20. There the one provoked is the LORD; the Hebrew has the divine name.

decisions.choice: the Lord's jealousy: his rightful claim to his people's whole loyalty, as a husband's claim on his wife
decisions.reason: God's jealousy is not petty envy but the love that will not share his people with other gods (Exodus 20:5; 34:14). Here "the Lord" is Christ, the Lord of the table (verse 21), to whom Paul gives what Scripture says of God.

decisions.choice: or: an alternative put as a warning question
decisions.reason: If they try to eat at both tables, are they daring the Lord to act, as Israel did?

decisions.choice: stir up the Lord's jealousy
decisions.reason: Balanced uses a plainer verb; "do we mean to" brings out the warning in the question.

records.source: μὴ ἰσχυρότεροι αὐτοῦ ἐσμεν;
records.gloss: Not stronger than him are we?
pieces: Do we think we are stronger than {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is?

L.22: We are not stronger than {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, are we?

R.22: Do we think we are stronger than the Lord?

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: μὴ shows that the answer must be no: no one can defy the Lord and escape his judgment.

decisions.choice: stronger: perhaps a jab at those who thought of themselves as strong
decisions.reason: In 4:10 Paul says with irony, "you are strong". Those who felt free to eat in idol temples may have counted themselves the strong, as opposed to the weak of chapter 8. Paul asks whether they are stronger than the Lord.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: A pronoun for the Lord. Readable names him.

records.source: Πάντα ἔξεστιν· ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει.
records.gloss: All things are lawful; but not all things are beneficial.
pieces: "Everything is permitted." Yes, but not everything is for the good.

L.23: "All things are permitted"; but not all things are of benefit.

R.23: Some of you say, "Everything is allowed." That may be true, but not everything is good for you.

decisions.choice: the Corinthian saying of 6:12, quoted again and marked as a quotation
alternatives: Paul's own principle, which he then limits
decisions.reason: As in 6:12 (12.s1, m1): the Greek has no quotation marks, but the same saying returns, again answered by Paul's "but". Here the saying lacks "to me", and Paul's answer measures freedom by the good of others (verse 24).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: no "to me" in the saying
alternatives: "all things are permitted to me", found in later manuscripts
decisions.reason: Later manuscripts add "to me" here, probably to match 6:12. The SBLGNT text governs. The evidence here is described from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: beneficial: doing real good, here above all to others
decisions.reason: As in 6:12. Verse 24 and verse 33 show that the good Paul has in mind is the good of others.

decisions.choice: permitted (L, B); allowed (R)
decisions.reason: The same words as 6:12, so the reader hears the saying return.

decisions.choice: Yes, but (B); Some of you say ... That may be true, but (R)
decisions.reason: As in 6:12 (r-en-2 there).

records.source: πάντα ἔξεστιν· ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα οἰκοδομεῖ.
records.gloss: All things are lawful; but not all things build up.
pieces: "Everything is permitted." Yes, but not everything builds others up.

L.23: "All things are permitted"; but not all things build up.

R.23: "Everything is allowed." Yes, but not everything makes others strong.

decisions.choice: the Corinthian saying again, marked as a quotation
decisions.reason: As in the first half of the verse (23.s1, m1).

decisions.choice: build up: strengthen others and the church
decisions.reason: οἰκοδομεῖ is the verb of 8:1: "knowledge puffs up, but love builds up". The test of freedom is whether it helps others grow.

decisions.choice: others
alternatives: no object, as in the Greek
decisions.reason: As in 8:1, Balanced and Readable supply the object to show who is built up.

decisions.choice: makes others strong
decisions.reason: As in 8:1 (Readable).

records.source: μηδεὶς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ζητείτω ἀλλὰ τὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου.
records.gloss: No one the of himself let seek but that of the other.
pieces: No one should look for {{gender:their|his}} own advantage, but for the other person's.

L.24: Let no one seek what is {{gender:their|his}} own, but what is the other's.

R.24: Do not think only about what is good for you. Think about what is good for other people.

decisions.choice: not one's own but the other's: put the good of others first
alternatives: never think of oneself at all
decisions.reason: The sharp "not ... but" sets priorities, as in Philippians 2:4. Verse 33 says the same of Paul: he seeks the good of many.

decisions.choice: the other: the other person, especially the fellow believer whose conscience is weak
decisions.reason: ἑτέρου is "the other one", whoever is affected. In this passage that includes the weak believer (8:9-13) and the unbeliever at a meal (verses 27-29).

decisions.choice: {{gender:their|his}}
decisions.reason: The command is for everyone, man or woman.

decisions.choice: only
decisions.reason: Readable shows that the contrast is about what comes first (m1).

records.source: πᾶν τὸ ἐν μακέλλῳ πωλούμενον ἐσθίετε μηδὲν ἀνακρίνοντες διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν, τοῦ κυρίου γὰρ ἡ γῆ καὶ τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῆς.
records.gloss: Everything that in meat market being sold eat, nothing examining on account of the conscience; \v 26 of the Lord for the earth and the fullness of it.
pieces: You may eat whatever is on sale in the meat market without asking questions for conscience' sake,
because "the earth belongs to the Lord, and everything that fills it."

L.25: Everything being sold in [the] meat market, eat, examining nothing for the sake of conscience;
L.26: for "the Lord's [is] the earth, and its fullness."

R.25: When you buy meat at the market, you can eat any of it. You do not need to ask where it came from to keep your conscience clear.
R.26: The Scriptures say, "The earth and everything in it belong to the Lord."

decisions.choice: the meat market: the city's market where meat and other food were sold
decisions.reason: μακέλλῳ is a market building for meat, fish and other food. Corinth had one, known from inscriptions. Some of the meat sold there came from temple sacrifices, and buyers could not always tell which.

decisions.choice: examining: asking questions about where the meat came from
decisions.reason: ἀνακρίνοντες is the verb of 2:14-15 and 4:3-4, to examine or inquire into. Paul tells them not to investigate the meat's history.

decisions.choice: for the sake of conscience: so that conscience will not be troubled
decisions.reason: There is no need to ask, since the food itself is clean (verse 26). Asking would only raise scruples where there need be none. Verses 28-29 show when conscience does come into it.

decisions.choice: a quotation of Psalm 24:1 (23:1 in the Greek Old Testament)
decisions.reason: The words match the Greek of the psalm. Where the Greek has κυρίου, the Hebrew has the divine name, YHWH. Later Jewish teaching used this verse to show that one should give thanks before eating, since all food belongs to God.

decisions.choice: eat: the imperative grants permission
alternatives: a command that everyone must eat
decisions.reason: Paul is not ordering them to eat but freeing them to eat whatever is sold.

decisions.choice: Lord
decisions.reason: Paul quotes the psalm with the Greek word for "Lord", so the text says "Lord", as in John 1:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:31; m4 notes the divine name in the Hebrew.

decisions.choice: You may eat ... without asking questions (B); you can eat ... You do not need to ask (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that the imperative grants permission (m5); "examine" (Literal) is kept for the courtroom sense in chapters 2 and 4.

decisions.choice: The Scriptures say
decisions.reason: Readable says that these words are a quotation.

records.source: εἴ τις καλεῖ ὑμᾶς τῶν ἀπίστων καὶ θέλετε πορεύεσθαι, πᾶν τὸ παρατιθέμενον ὑμῖν ἐσθίετε μηδὲν ἀνακρίνοντες διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν·
records.gloss: If anyone invites you of the unbelievers and you want to go, everything being set before you eat, nothing examining on account of the conscience;
pieces: Suppose an unbeliever asks you to dinner and you decide to go. Then eat whatever is served, and do not ask questions for conscience' sake.

L.27: If any of the unbelievers invites you and you want to go, eat everything set before you, examining nothing for the sake of conscience.

R.27: Someone who does not believe in Jesus may invite you to a meal at their home. If you want to go, eat whatever food they give you. You do not need to ask where it came from to keep your conscience clear.

decisions.choice: a meal in a private home, not in a temple
alternatives: a meal in a temple dining room
decisions.reason: Verses 14-22 have ruled out meals at an idol's table. Here the setting is a meal served by an unbelieving host, where the food might or might not come from a sacrifice.

decisions.choice: unbelievers: people outside the church
decisions.reason: ἀπίστων is used throughout this letter for those who do not believe (6:6; 7:12-15; 14:22-24).

decisions.choice: and you want to go: Paul neither commands nor forbids accepting
decisions.reason: Accepting such an invitation is left to the believer.

decisions.choice: examining nothing for the sake of conscience: as in verse 25
decisions.reason: See 25.s1, m2 and m3.

decisions.choice: does not believe in Jesus; at their home
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the unbelievers are and makes the setting explicit (m1).

decisions.choice: asks you to dinner
decisions.reason: The invitation is to a meal, as the rest of the verse shows.

records.source: ἐὰν δέ τις ὑμῖν εἴπῃ· Τοῦτο ἱερόθυτόν ἐστιν, μὴ ἐσθίετε δι’ ἐκεῖνον τὸν μηνύσαντα καὶ τὴν συνείδησιν·
records.gloss: If but anyone to you says: This sacrificed-to-a-god is, not eat on account of that [one] having informed and the conscience;
pieces: But if anyone points out to you, "This came from a temple sacrifice," leave it uneaten. Do so out of regard for the person who pointed it out, and because of conscience.

L.28: But if anyone says to you, "This is [meat] offered in sacrifice," do not eat [it], because of that one who informed [you] and because of conscience.

R.28: But someone may say to you, "This meat was offered to a god." Then do not eat it. Do this for the sake of the person who told you, and because of that person's conscience.

decisions.choice: offered in sacrifice: the polite word for sacrificial meat, used by a non-Jew
decisions.reason: ἱερόθυτόν means "offered in a sacred rite". Elsewhere Paul uses εἰδωλόθυτον, "offered to idols", the word Jews and Christians used (8:1, m2). The polite word suggests that the speaker is not a believer, or is speaking in a pagan setting.

decisions.choice: the one who informed you: probably a fellow guest or the host, perhaps a believer with a weak conscience
decisions.reason: Paul does not say who it is. The polite word fits an unbeliever who assumes that a Christian would care; a weak believer is also possible. Either way, eating after being told would seem to approve of idol worship in that person's eyes.

decisions.choice: because of conscience: the other person's conscience, as verse 29 explains
decisions.reason: The believer's own conscience is not at stake; the informer's is (verse 29).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: the verse ends with "and conscience"
alternatives: the words of Psalm 24:1 repeated at the end, "for the earth is the Lord's and its fullness", found in later manuscripts
decisions.reason: Later manuscripts repeat the quotation of verse 26 here. It is missing from the early manuscripts and adds nothing to the sense. The SBLGNT text governs. The evidence here is described from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: [meat] offered in sacrifice (L); came from a temple sacrifice (B); offered to a god (R)
decisions.reason: The phrase "food offered to idols" is kept for the Christian word (terms doc). Here the speaker uses a different, neutral word, so a different phrase is used.

decisions.choice: that person's conscience
decisions.reason: Readable makes explicit whose conscience is meant, as verse 29 says (m3).

decisions.choice: leave it uneaten
decisions.reason: The sense is the same; the wording marks the change from verse 27.

records.source: συνείδησιν δὲ λέγω οὐχὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀλλὰ τὴν τοῦ ἑτέρου· ἱνατί γὰρ ἡ ἐλευθερία μου κρίνεται ὑπὸ ἄλλης συνειδήσεως;
records.gloss: Conscience but I say not the of yourself but that of the other; why for the freedom of me is judged by another conscience?
pieces: By conscience I mean the other person's, not yours. For why should another person's conscience pass judgment on my freedom?

L.29: Now I say conscience, not your own, but that of the other; for why is my freedom judged by another conscience?

R.29: I mean the other person's conscience, not yours. Why should my freedom be judged by what someone else's conscience says?

decisions.choice: whose conscience: the conscience of the one who informed, not the believer's own
decisions.reason: Paul explains verse 28. The believer refrains for the other's sake, not because his own conscience forbids the food.

decisions.choice: why is my freedom judged: Paul explains that his own freedom is not bound by another's conscience; he gives up eating only out of love
alternatives: an objection from a Corinthian, which Paul quotes
why give anyone the chance to condemn my freedom? that is, I refrain so as not to be condemned
decisions.reason: The question with γὰρ is hard to connect. Read with verse 28, it says that the believer does not change his own conviction: his freedom remains, and he holds it back only for the other person. Some read the question as a Corinthian protest that Paul answers in verses 31-33; others as Paul's reason for not giving offense. The words do not settle it.

decisions.choice: freedom: the believer's freedom to eat any food
decisions.reason: ἐλευθερία is the freedom Paul claimed for himself in 9:1, 19.

decisions.choice: By conscience I mean
decisions.reason: Balanced makes the explanation clear.

records.source: εἰ ἐγὼ χάριτι μετέχω, τί βλασφημοῦμαι ὑπὲρ οὗ ἐγὼ εὐχαριστῶ;
records.gloss: If I with thanks partake, why am I slandered for that which I give thanks?
pieces: If I eat my share with gratitude, why should anyone speak evil of me over food for which I thank God?

L.30: If I share [in the food] with thanks, why am I spoken evil of because of that for which I give thanks?

R.30: I thank God for my food when I eat it. So why should anyone say bad things about me because of food I have thanked God for?

decisions.choice: thanks: gratitude to God for the food
decisions.reason: χάριτι usually means grace, but here it means thanks, as the verb εὐχαριστῶ, "I give thanks", shows. The same use is found in 15:57 and 2 Corinthians 2:14.

decisions.choice: spoken evil of: denounced, condemned by others
decisions.reason: βλασφημοῦμαι is to speak against someone, to slander. Someone who sees a believer eat sacrificial food might condemn him as an idolater.

decisions.choice: a second question, continuing verse 29
decisions.reason: It shares the uncertainty of verse 29 (29.s1, m2): it may express Paul's own freedom, which he holds back for others, or a protest he goes on to answer.

decisions.choice: thanks (L); gratitude (B); thank God (R)
decisions.reason: χάρις is a key term, normally "grace", but here the sense is thanks (m1).

decisions.choice: [in the food]
decisions.reason: The verb means to have a share in something; Literal supplies what is shared.

records.source: Εἴτε οὖν ἐσθίετε εἴτε πίνετε εἴτε τι ποιεῖτε, πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ ποιεῖτε.
records.gloss: Whether then you eat or you drink or something you do, all things to glory of God do.
pieces: So then, when you eat, when you drink, whatever you do, do everything for God's glory.

L.31: Whether, then, you eat or you drink or you do anything, do all things for [the] glory of God.

R.31: So in everything you do, even in eating and drinking, live in a way that brings glory to God.

decisions.choice: then: the conclusion of the whole discussion begun in 8:1
decisions.reason: οὖν gathers up chapters 8-10: the question of food is settled not by rules alone but by the aim of all one does.

decisions.choice: glory of God: God's greatness honored and made known
decisions.reason: δόξαν is God's own splendor, and to do something "for" it is to act so that he is honored and praised. Eating, drinking and every other act can do that.

decisions.choice: eating and drinking: the everyday acts this discussion has been about
decisions.reason: Paul starts from the food and drink in question and widens it to everything.

decisions.choice: even in eating and drinking; live in a way that
decisions.reason: Readable shows that ordinary acts are included, and puts "do" as a way of living.

records.source: ἀπρόσκοποι καὶ Ἰουδαίοις γίνεσθε καὶ Ἕλλησιν καὶ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ, καθὼς κἀγὼ πάντα πᾶσιν ἀρέσκω, μὴ ζητῶν τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ σύμφορον ἀλλὰ τὸ τῶν πολλῶν, ἵνα σωθῶσιν.
records.gloss: Without causing stumbling both to Jews become and to Greeks and to the church of the God, \v 33 as I also in all things all please, not seeking the of myself benefit but that of the many, so that they may be saved.
pieces: Do not trip anyone up, not Jews, not Greeks, not the church of God.
I do the same: in all I do I seek to please all people, looking not for what helps me but for what helps the many, so that they may be saved.

L.32: Become people who cause no stumbling, both to Jews and to Greeks and to the church of God,
L.33: just as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking the benefit of myself but that of the many, in order that they may be saved.

R.32: Do not do anything that would make people fall into sin, whether they are Jews or people who are not Jews or members of God's church.
R.33: That is how I live. I try to please all people in all I do. I do not look for what is good for me. I look for what is good for many people, so that they will be saved.

decisions.choice: causing no stumbling: giving no one a reason to fall into sin or turn away
decisions.reason: ἀπρόσκοποι can mean "blameless" (Philippians 1:10), but here it is set beside Jews, Greeks and the church as people who could be tripped up, so the active sense fits. It recalls the stumbling block of 8:9.

decisions.choice: Jews, Greeks and the church of God: everyone the believer has to do with
decisions.reason: Paul divides humanity into Jews and Greeks, that is, non-Jews (1:22-24), and adds the church, made up of both. Believers should not put an obstacle in the way of any of them.

decisions.choice: please: fit in with others for their good, not flatter them
decisions.reason: ἀρέσκω here means to serve the interests of others, as 9:19-22 describes; in Galatians 1:10 Paul refuses to please people in the sense of seeking their approval. The next words show the aim: their good, so that they may be saved.

decisions.choice: benefit ... of the many: what helps the many
decisions.reason: σύμφορον picks up the "benefit" of verse 23. "The many" is everyone else, as against Paul himself.

decisions.choice: that they may be saved: that they may come to faith and be kept in it to the end
decisions.reason: As in 9:22, Paul's purpose in giving up his rights is the salvation of others.

decisions.choice: Do not trip anyone up
decisions.reason: "Give offense" now suggests hurt feelings; the terms doc uses "trip up" for this stumbling picture.

decisions.choice: people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: "Greeks" here means all non-Jews, as in 1:22-24; Readable says so.

decisions.choice: I do the same (B); That is how I live (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable start a new sentence at verse 33 and keep its link with verse 32.
